1: Open by framing this as a practical onboarding session for engineers who must connect control behavior to reviewable evidence. The deck uses one small pitch-rate limiter as the recurring example, then scales to a feedback loop, mode logic, model references, tests, and evidence handling. Every delivered model is an illustrative training model using representative values, not production aircraft data. Set expectations that the HIL and Jenkins sections explain concepts only: this project executed desktop simulations and did not use HIL hardware or a Jenkins agent. The session is designed for approximately 45–60 minutes, with questions at the major section transitions.
2: Use this slide to explain why an executable model can become a shared engineering reference. Requirements provide intent, control design provides the law, simulation exposes time behavior, and verification checks observables against acceptance criteria. The important word is shared: each discipline still owns its work products and reviews. A model does not replace requirements, plans, configuration management, or independent verification. In the delivered project, the same PitchRateLimiter behavior is visible in the model, exercised by the harness, checked in MATLAB assessments, and summarized in retained results.
3: Preview the learning path. First, learners read model structure and timing. Second, they build and review a small control component. Third, they make expectations executable with a harness and assessments. Fourth, they integrate referenced models and controlled interfaces. Finally, they interpret automation and HIL outputs as evidence inputs rather than approvals. Encourage learners to ask two questions on every artifact: what requirement justifies this element, and what objective result demonstrates it? The project traceability CSV provides a concrete version of that habit for PRL-001 through PRL-005.
4: Emphasize that MATLAB and Simulink are complementary parts of one environment. MATLAB is convenient for data preparation, algorithms, automation, analysis, and reporting. Simulink makes time-based signal flow, hierarchy, state, interfaces, and sample times visible and executable. The delivered scripts use MATLAB to generate, configure, simulate, test, and export the Simulink models. This is useful for repeatability: another engineer can regenerate the same artifacts without manually rebuilding diagrams. The distinction is about the best representation for the job, not competing tools.

7:
Explain the small modeling vocabulary: libraries provide controlled reusable content, blocks perform operations or represent dynamics, signals carry typed values, and subsystems organize behavior behind an interface. Buses group related interface data; data dictionaries persist model-relevant design data. In the delivered project, FlightControlBus groups q_rate, pitch_angle, mach, air_data_valid, and mode, while FCS_Data.sldd stores its definition and controlled gains. A bus is an interface contract; it does not by itself guarantee semantic correctness.

12:
Maintain the certification distinction carefully. FAA AC 20-115D recognizes DO-178C as an acceptable means, but not the only means, for showing compliance with applicable airworthiness regulations. It also recognizes DO-331 as the Model-Based Development and Verification Supplement to DO-178C and DO-278A. Neither document makes a model automatically compliant. The approved plans define how models are used—as specification, design, source, or verification material—and which objectives, reviews, independence, configuration, and evidence apply. Avoid saying that software receives a standalone DO-178C certificate.

14:
Traceability is valuable because it makes each artifact explainable in both directions. A requirement should identify its implementing model element and objective verification; a model element and test should have a justified requirement. The evidence package also needs controlled procedures, results, configuration, reviews, coverage or analyses where applicable, and problem dispositions. FAA software-approval guidance treats certification credit as authority acceptance of lifecycle data and other evidence. Therefore a green pipeline or test result is an input to review—not approval on its own.

[Sources]
- https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Order/FAA_Order_8110.49A.pdf
15: Use this as a representative development sequence, not a universal process prescription. Planning and the objective set come before implementation. Requirements allocate observable behavior and interfaces. The component model is then built under controlled data and reviewed against model standards. Unit-test design follows the requirement, not the block diagram. In a Simulink Test environment, definitions may be organized in .mldatx; this computer lacks that product, so the delivered training workflow uses a standalone harness and MATLAB assessment suite. The principle—controlled, reviewable, repeatable verification—remains the same.
16:
Continue from component verification into architecture integration and automation. Update/compile is a semantic consistency gate: model references, buses, types, dimensions, parameters, and sample times must agree. A pipeline can make those checks repeatable, but a pass is not certification approval. The failure loop matters: reproduce, isolate the first meaningful cause, correct it, add regression protection, and rerun the controlled scope. HIL appears as a later program activity; no Jenkins pipeline or HIL campaign was executed for this desktop training project.

17: Compare the levels of requirement detail. The system statement describes desired aircraft behavior. The interface statement makes units, sign, range, and rate explicit. The component statement defines the inclusive magnitude clamp. The derived statement highlights behavior or interface information that may require feedback to system or safety processes. A testable requirement names the observable output, tolerance, timing, applicable modes, and invalid-input behavior. In this project, the training fallback is explicitly zero command when either normal_mode or input_valid is false.

21: Use these practices as a review checklist. Names should communicate engineering meaning. Signal contracts should expose units, types, dimensions, sample times, range, validity, and ownership. Inputs should enter consistently and outputs should leave consistently. Hierarchy should let a reviewer summarize one level quickly, then open the next level for detail. Reuse through libraries and model references should have controlled ownership. 23: Walk through the test classes as requirement-driven coverage. Nominal cases prove the limiter does not modify valid in-range commands. Exact-boundary cases prove inclusivity. Just-outside and large values prove clamping. Mode and validity cases prove the documented fallback. Timing cases prove the model configuration and output sampling at 50 Hz. Then discuss interactions: mode, validity, boundary, and transition combinations can reveal defects missed by one-dimensional tests. The delivered executable suite records actual and expected values plus the active flag and numeric error.

27:
Treat this as a CI concept slide; no Jenkins run occurred in this project. A pipeline can orchestrate controlled startup, model update, checks, executable tests, and report retention. MATLAB and Simulink do the engineering operations; Jenkins or another orchestrator schedules them and captures artifacts. A passing pipeline means the configured steps passed on that agent and configuration. It is evidence input, not certification approval, and it does not replace review of skipped tests, warnings, configuration, coverage, traceability, or unresolved problem reports.

[Sources]
- https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Order/FAA_Order_8110.49A.pdf
28: Start with reproducibility. If the failure does not reproduce locally under the controlled command, compare agent software, licenses, paths, project startup, data, and versions. If update/compile fails, inspect interface, type, dimension, rate, model-reference, parameter, and variant diagnostics. If simulation or assessment fails, compare stimulus, expected result, tolerance, mode, initial state, and timing. Fix the root cause, add a focused regression check, rerun the affected scope, then run the controlled full set. Do not hide warnings merely to create a green result.
29: This slide defines a real HIL arrangement in general terms: actual controller hardware and physical I/O interact with a real-time plant simulation. That distinction matters. A desktop Simulink simulation, including the models delivered here, is not completed HIL evidence. HIL campaigns also need controlled hardware/software configuration, I/O calibration, timing, scenarios, expected results, logs, review, and problem disposition. Use the diagram to identify which parts must be real hardware and which are simulated. No HIL hardware was available or used for this training project.
30: HIL pass criteria must be numeric and reviewable: functional tolerance, timing allocation, interface freshness and status, fault-response timing, and retained configuration/evidence. A visually smooth trace is not a pass criterion. The 50 Hz limiter checks in this project illustrate discrete timing on a desktop model only; they do not measure target processor execution, I/O latency, jitter, or overrun under worst-case load. Those claims require the actual HIL or target environment and controlled measurements. No HIL result is presented in this deck.
